items.title: Quiz Q#1 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of Geoffrey Chaucer in the chronological order of their composition:
(A) The Canterbury Tales
(B) The Book of the Duchess
(C) The Legend of Good Women
(D) The House of Fame
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Chaucer wrote The Book of the Duchess first (c. 1368-1369) during his French Period on the death of Blanche of Lancaster. Next came The House of Fame (c. 1379-1380) and The Legend of Good Women (c. 1385-1386) during his Italian Period. He began The Canterbury Tales last (c. 1387-1400) during his English Period.

items.title: Quiz Q#2 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Match List I (Critic) with List II (Famous Comment on Geoffrey Chaucer):
List I:
(A) John Dryden
(B) Edmund Spenser
(C) Matthew Arnold
(D) G. K. Chesterton

List II:
(I) "Chaucer lacks not only the accent of Dante, but also the high seriousness."
(II) "Here is God's plenty."
(III) "If Chaucer is the father of English poetry, he is the grandfather of the English novel."
(IV) "Well of English undefiled."

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: John Dryden wrote 'Here is God's plenty' in his Preface to Fables (1700). Edmund Spenser called Chaucer 'well of English undefiled' in The Faerie Queene. Matthew Arnold noted in The Study of Poetry (1880) that Chaucer lacked 'high seriousness'. G. K. Chesterton called him the 'grandfather of the English novel'.

items.title: Quiz Q#3 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Which four pilgrims in the General Prologue to The Canterbury Tales are idealized by Geoffrey Chaucer without any irony or satire?
(A) The Knight
(B) The Monk
(C) The Parson
(D) The Plowman
(E) The Clerk of Oxford
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Chaucer presents four characters as ideal models of their social estates without satirizing them: The Knight (chivalry), The Parson (faithful village clergy), The Plowman (honest Christian laborer), and The Clerk of Oxford (devoted scholar). The Monk is satirized as a fat, worldly hunter who ignores his cloister rules.

items.title: Quiz Q#4 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: In The Canterbury Tales, Harry Bailly proposes that each pilgrim tell four stories in total, two on the way to Canterbury and two on the return journey, which would have totaled 120 stories.
Statement II: Only two tales in The Canterbury Tales are written in prose: The Tale of Melibee and The Parson's Tale.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
items.explanation: Both statements are true. In the General Prologue, the Host Harry Bailly suggests 4 tales per pilgrim (2 going, 2 returning = 120 tales for 30 pilgrims), though Chaucer completed only 24. The only two prose tales are Chaucer's own second tale (The Tale of Melibee) and The Parson's Tale.

items.title: Quiz Q#5 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which pilgrim in Chaucer's General Prologue wears a golden brooch inscribed with a crowned 'A' and the Latin motto 'Amor Vincit Omnia' (Love conquers all)?
items.explanation: Madame Eglantine, the Prioress, wears a coral rosary with a shining gold brooch engraved with 'A' and 'Amor Vincit Omnia' (Love conquers all), highlighting the gentle irony between her religious vows and her courtly, worldly manners.

items.title: Quiz Q#6 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: About which pilgrim does Chaucer write: 'For gold in phisik is a cordial, / Therefore he lovede gold in special'?
items.explanation: Chaucer jokes that because potable gold (aurum potabile) was used in medieval medicine as a heart tonic ('cordial'), the Doctor of Physic had a special love for hoarding the gold he earned during plague outbreaks.

items.title: Quiz Q#7 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Match List I (Chaucer's Work) with List II (Poetic Meter / Stanza Form):
List I:
(A) The Book of the Duchess
(B) Troilus and Criseyde
(C) The Legend of Good Women
(D) The Tale of Melibee

List II:
(I) Rhyme Royal (7-line stanza, abab bcc)
(II) First English use of Heroic Couplets
(III) Octosyllabic Couplets (8-syllable lines)
(IV) Moral Prose Treatise

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Book of the Duchess (1369) and The House of Fame are written in 8-syllable octosyllabic couplets. Troilus and Criseyde and The Parliament of Foules use the 7-line Rhyme Royal stanza. The Legend of Good Women marks Chaucer's first use of Heroic Couplets. The Tale of Melibee is in prose.

items.title: Quiz Q#8 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): Chaucer wrote The Legend of Good Women at the command of the God of Love and Queen Alceste (representing Queen Anne of Bohemia).
Reason (R): It was framed as a comic penance for having portrayed woman's infidelity in Troilus and Criseyde and his translation of The Romaunt of the Rose.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
items.explanation: In the Prologue to The Legend of Good Women, the God of Love scolds Chaucer for translating the satirical Roman de la Rose and writing about Criseyde's betrayal of Troilus. Queen Alceste defends him and assigns him the penance of writing legends of faithful ancient women betrayed by men.

items.title: Quiz Q#9 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which pilgrim joins the Canterbury company late along the road at Boughton-under-Blean after his master flees in shame?
items.explanation: Near Boughton-under-Blean, a black-clad Canon and his Yeoman gallop up to overtake the pilgrims. When the Yeoman begins exposing his master's alchemical tricks, the Canon flees in shame, and the Canon's Yeoman stays as the 32nd member to tell his tale.

items.stem:

(III) Palamon, Arcite, and Emily
(IV) Carpenter John, Alison, Nicholas, and Absolon

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Knight's Tale follows Theban cousins Palamon and Arcite competing for Emily. The Miller's Tale features carpenter John, his young wife Alison, student Nicholas, and clerk Absolon. The Merchant's Tale tells of old blind knight January, young May, and squire Damian in the pear tree. The Nun's Priest's Tale is the beast fable of rooster Chauntecleer, hen Pertelote, and the fox.

items.title: Quiz Q#11 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which two tales in The Canterbury Tales are left unfinished (broken off mid-story)?
options: The Reeve's Tale and The Manciple's Tale
The Knight's Tale and The Miller's Tale
The Cook's Tale and The Squire's Tale (plus Chaucer's interrupted Tale of Sir Thopas)
The Pardoner's Tale and The Friar's Tale
items.explanation: The Cook's Tale breaks off after 58 lines about Perkyn Reveller. The Squire's Oriental romance about Princess Canacee's magic ring is left unfinished (interrupted by the Franklin), and Chaucer's own parody Sir Thopas is stopped by the Host Harry Bailly.

items.title: Quiz Q#12 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Chaucer's elegy The Book of the Duchess (1368-1369) was written to mourn the death of:
options: Queen Anne of Bohemia (wife of King Richard II)
Philippa of Hainault (wife of King Edward III)
Blanche, Duchess of Lancaster (first wife of John of Gaunt)
items.explanation: The Book of the Duchess was written in 1368-1369 to console Chaucer's patron John of Gaunt (represented as the Man in Black) after his young wife Blanche, Duchess of Lancaster ('White'), died of the plague.

items.title: Quiz Q#13 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which work of Chaucer is an unfinished dream vision in three books where a talking Golden Eagle carries the poet 'Geffrey' into the sky to visit a palace built on a rock of ice?
items.explanation: In Book II of The House of Fame (c. 1379-1380), a talkative Golden Eagle (inspired by Dante's Purgatorio) carries Geffrey up to the House of Fame, which stands on a melting rock of ice where famous names slowly fade away.

items.title: Quiz Q#14 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Who coined the critical term 'The Marriage Group' in 1912 to describe the debate on marriage conducted across the tales of the Wife of Bath, the Clerk, the Merchant, and the Franklin?
items.explanation: Harvard scholar George Lyman Kittredge introduced the famous critical concept of the 'Marriage Group' in 1912, showing how the Wife of Bath (female sovereignty), the Clerk (complete wifely obedience in Griselda), the Merchant (bitter satire of marriage), and the Franklin (mutual love and generosity) form a dramatic debate.

items.title: Quiz Q#15 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Chaucer's tragic verse romance Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385) is primarily adapted from which work by Giovanni Boccaccio?
items.explanation: Chaucer adapted Troilus and Criseyde from Boccaccio's Italian poem Il Filostrato, while deepening the psychology of Criseyde and turning her cousin Pandaro into her humorous, scheming uncle Pandarus. (Boccaccio's Teseida was the source for The Knight's Tale).
