items.explanation: Chronology in Early Middle English & Anglo-Norman: Historia Regum Britanniae (1136), Ormulum (1170), Brut (1190), and The Divine Comedy (1308).

items.title: Quiz Q#41 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem:
Arrange the following landmark works of the The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) in chronological order of their publication:
(A) Havelok the Dane by Anonymous — Beowulf
(B) Canzoniere by Petrarch
(C) Decameron by Giovanni Boccaccio
(D) Cleanness by Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.explanation: Chronology in The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century): Havelok the Dane (1280), Canzoniere (1327), Decameron (1349), and Cleanness (1350).

items.title: Quiz Q#42 · John Mandeville
items.stem:
Arrange the following landmark works of the The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) in chronological order of their publication:
(A) Mandeville's Travels by John Mandeville
(B) Piers Plowman by William Langland
(C) Mirour de l’Omme by John Gower
(D) Vox Clamantis by John Gower
items.explanation: Chronology in The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century): Mandeville's Travels (1357), Piers Plowman (1360), Mirour de l’Omme (1376), and Vox Clamantis (1381).

items.title: Quiz Q#43 · John Wycliffe
items.stem:
Arrange the following landmark works of the The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) in chronological order of their publication:
(A) English Bible associated with the Wycliffite translations by John Wycliffe
(B) Confessio Amantis by John Gower
(C) The Canterbury Tales by Geoffrey Chaucer
(D) The Parliament of Fowls by Geoffrey Chaucer
items.explanation: Chronology in The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century): English Bible associated with the Wycliffite translations (1382), Confessio Amantis (1390), The Canterbury Tales (1476), and The Parliament of Fowls (1478).

items.title: Quiz Q#44 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Arrange the following landmark works of the The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) in chronological order of their publication:
(A) Troilus and Criseyde by Geoffrey Chaucer
(B) The House of Fame by Geoffrey Chaucer
(C) William Caxton’s edition of Le Morte Darthur by William Caxton
(D) The Fall of Princes by John Lydgate
items.explanation: Chronology in The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century): Troilus and Criseyde (1483), The House of Fame (1484), William Caxton’s edition of Le Morte Darthur (1485), and The Fall of Princes (1494).

items.title: Quiz Q#45 · Margery Kempe
items.stem:
Arrange the following landmark works of the The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) in chronological order of their publication:
(A) The Book of Margery Kempe by Margery Kempe
(B) The Book of the Duchess by Geoffrey Chaucer
(C) Revelations of Divine Love by Julian of Norwich
(D) Sir Gawain and the Green Knight by Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.explanation: Chronology in The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century): The Book of Margery Kempe (1501), The Book of the Duchess (1532), Revelations of Divine Love (1670), and Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (1839).

items.title: Quiz Q#46 · John Lydgate
items.stem:
Arrange the following landmark works of the 15th-Century Transition, Drama & Early Print in chronological order of their publication:
(A) The Complaint of the Black Knight by John Lydgate
(B) La Male Regle by Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
(C) The Regiment of Princes by Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
(D) The Complaint by Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.explanation: Chronology in 15th-Century Transition, Drama & Early Print: The Complaint of the Black Knight (1402), La Male Regle (1405), The Regiment of Princes (1411), and The Complaint (1419).

items.title: Quiz Q#47 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem:
Arrange the following landmark works of the 15th-Century Transition, Drama & Early Print in chronological order of their publication:
(A) Dialogue with a Friend by Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
(B) The Temple of Glass by John Lydgate
(C) Le Morte Darthur by Thomas Malory
(D) Phyllyp Sparowe by John Skelton
items.explanation: Chronology in 15th-Century Transition, Drama & Early Print: Dialogue with a Friend (1420), The Temple of Glass (1476), Le Morte Darthur (1485), and Phyllyp Sparowe (1505).

items.title: Quiz Q#48 · John Skelton
items.stem:
Arrange the following landmark works of the Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation in chronological order of their publication:
(A) The Bowge of Court by John Skelton
(B) The Ship of Fools by Alexander Barclay
(C) Praise of Folly by Desiderius Erasmus
(D) Utopia by Thomas More
items.explanation: Chronology in Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation: The Bowge of Court (1499), The Ship of Fools (1509), Praise of Folly (1511), and Utopia (1516).

items.title: Quiz Q#49 · Cynewulf
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Cynewulf?
(A) Christ II
(B) Elene
(C) Juliana
(D) The Wanderer
items.explanation: Christ II, Elene, and Juliana are canonical works authored by Cynewulf. The Wanderer is not by Cynewulf.

items.title: Quiz Q#50 · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Ælfric of Eynsham?
(A) Catholic Homilies
(B) Grammar
(C) Lives of Saints
(D) Sermo Lupi ad Anglos
items.explanation: Catholic Homilies, Grammar, and Lives of Saints are canonical works authored by Ælfric of Eynsham. Sermo Lupi ad Anglos is not by Ælfric of Eynsham.

items.title: Quiz Q#51 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem:
Which of the following are major Old English elegiac poems preserved in the Exeter Book?
(A) The Wanderer
(B) The Seafarer
(C) The Wife’s Lament
(D) Havelok the Dane
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Wanderer, The Seafarer, and The Wife's Lament are celebrated Old English elegies preserved in the Exeter Book. Havelok the Dane is a later Middle English romance.

items.title: Quiz Q#52 · John Gower
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by John Gower?
(A) Confessio Amantis
(B) Mirour de l’Omme
(C) Vox Clamantis
(D) Piers Plowman
items.explanation: Confessio Amantis, Mirour de l’Omme, and Vox Clamantis are canonical works authored by John Gower. Piers Plowman is not by John Gower.

items.title: Quiz Q#53 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Anonymous — Gawain Poet?
(A) Cleanness
(B) Patience
(C) Pearl
(D) Confessio Amantis
items.explanation: Cleanness, Patience, and Pearl are canonical works authored by Anonymous — Gawain Poet. Confessio Amantis is not by Anonymous — Gawain Poet.

items.title: Quiz Q#54 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)?
(A) Dialogue with a Friend
(B) La Male Regle
(C) The Complaint
(D) The Fall of Princes
items.explanation: Dialogue with a Friend, La Male Regle, and The Complaint are canonical works authored by Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve). The Fall of Princes is not by Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve).

items.title: Quiz Q#55 · John Lydgate
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by John Lydgate?
(A) The Fall of Princes
(B) The Complaint of the Black Knight
(C) The Story of Thebes
(D) The Regiment of Princes
items.explanation: The Fall of Princes, The Complaint of the Black Knight, and The Story of Thebes are canonical works authored by John Lydgate. The Regiment of Princes is not by John Lydgate.

items.title: Quiz Q#56 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by Geoffrey Chaucer?
(A) The Book of the Duchess
(B) The Canterbury Tales
(C) The House of Fame
(D) The Temple of Glass
items.explanation: The Book of the Duchess, The Canterbury Tales, and The House of Fame are canonical works authored by Geoffrey Chaucer. The Temple of Glass is not by Geoffrey Chaucer.

items.title: Quiz Q#57 · William Caxton
items.stem:
Which of the following works were translated and/or published by William Caxton at his press?
(A) Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye
(B) The Game and Playe of the Chesse
(C) The Dictes and Sayenges of the Phylosophres
(D) The Pastime of Pleasure
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (1473–1474), The Game and Playe of the Chesse (1474), and The Dictes and Sayenges of the Phylosophres (1477) are landmark works translated and printed by Caxton. The Pastime of Pleasure is by Stephen Hawes (1509).

items.title: Quiz Q#58 · John Skelton
items.stem:
Which of the following works were written by John Skelton?
(A) Colin Clout
(B) Phyllyp Sparowe
(C) Speke, Parrot
(D) The Steele Glas
items.explanation: Colin Clout, Phyllyp Sparowe, and Speke, Parrot are canonical works authored by John Skelton. The Steele Glas is not by John Skelton.

items.title: Quiz Q#59 · King Alfred the Great
items.meta: The Medieval Age · King Alfred the Great
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding King Alfred the Great:
Statement I: King Alfred initiated a major educational and translation revival in late 9th-century Wessex.
Statement II: King Alfred personally translated Pope Gregory the Great’s Pastoral Care (Cura Pastoralis) into Old English.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are correct: King Alfred initiated an ambitious educational revival in the late 9th century and translated Gregory's Pastoral Care into English prose for his bishops.

items.title: Quiz Q#60 · Cynewulf
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Cynewulf:
Statement I: Cynewulf wove runic signatures into four surviving Old English poems: Christ II, Elene, Juliana, and The Fates of the Apostles.
Statement II: Elene is an important narrative poem by Cynewulf recounting Saint Helena’s discovery of the True Cross.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
items.explanation: Both statements are correct: Cynewulf signed four Old English poems using runes, and Elene is his longest poem, celebrating the Invention of the Cross.

items.title: Quiz Q#61 · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Ælfric of Eynsham:
Statement I: Catholic Homilies was composed by Ælfric in two series around 990–995 CE.
Statement II: Grammar is an important pedagogical work by Ælfric of Eynsham written to teach Latin to English novices.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are correct: Ælfric wrote the Catholic Homilies (c. 990–995) and the Grammar (c. 995) as part of the late Anglo-Saxon monastic revival.

items.title: Quiz Q#62 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Old English heroic and visionary poetry:
Statement I: The Battle of Maldon commemorates the defeat and death of Ealdorman Byrhtnoth in 991 CE.
Statement II: The Dream of the Rood is an important religious dream-vision preserved in the Vercelli Book.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are correct: The Battle of Maldon records the historical clash of 991 CE, and The Dream of the Rood is a supreme Old English visionary poem preserved in the Vercelli Book.

items.title: Quiz Q#63 · John Gower
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding John Gower:
Statement I: Confessio Amantis was completed by John Gower around 1390.
Statement II: Mirour de l’Omme is an important moral allegorical work by John Gower written in Anglo-Norman French.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are correct: Gower completed his English poem Confessio Amantis c. 1390, and wrote Mirour de l'Omme in French and Vox Clamantis in Latin.

items.title: Quiz Q#64 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding the Anonymous Gawain Poet:
Statement I: Pearl, Cleanness, Patience, and Sir Gawain and the Green Knight survive in a single unique manuscript (MS Cotton Nero A.x).
Statement II: Patience is an important alliterative poem by the Gawain Poet retelling the biblical story of Jonah.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
items.explanation: Both statements are correct: The four masterworks of the Gawain Poet survive uniquely in British Library MS Cotton Nero A.x, and Patience retells the Book of Jonah.

items.title: Quiz Q#65 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve):
Statement I: The Regiment of Princes was composed in 1411 for Prince Henry, the future Henry V.
Statement II: La Male Regle is an important autobiographical confession by Thomas Hoccleve.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are correct: Hoccleve composed The Regiment of Princes in 1411 containing his famous eulogy of Chaucer, and La Male Regle (1405) confessing his misrule.

items.title: Quiz Q#66 · John Lydgate
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding John Lydgate:
Statement I: The Fall of Princes was composed by John Lydgate between 1431 and 1438 for Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester.
Statement II: The Complaint of the Black Knight is an important courtly love vision by John Lydgate.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are correct: Lydgate wrote The Fall of Princes (1431–1438) based on Boccaccio, and The Complaint of the Black Knight in imitation of Chaucer.

items.title: Quiz Q#67 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding Geoffrey Chaucer:
Statement I: The Book of the Duchess was composed c. 1368–1369 as an elegy on the death of Blanche of Lancaster.
Statement II: The Canterbury Tales is an important work by Geoffrey Chaucer framed around a pilgrimage to Saint Thomas Becket's shrine.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are correct: Chaucer composed The Book of the Duchess (c. 1368–1369) for John of Gaunt on the loss of his wife, and The Canterbury Tales in the 1380s–1390s.

items.title: Quiz Q#68 · William Caxton
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding William Caxton:
Statement I: William Caxton established England's first printing press at Westminster in 1476.
Statement II: Caxton published Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte Darthur in 1485, dividing it into twenty-one books.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
items.explanation: Both statements are correct: Caxton introduced movable-type printing to England in 1476 and printed Malory's Le Morte Darthur in 1485.

items.title: Quiz Q#69 · John Skelton
items.stem:
Given below are two statements regarding John Skelton:
Statement I: Colin Clout was composed by John Skelton around 1522 as a satire against Cardinal Wolsey.
Statement II: Phyllyp Sparowe is an important mock-elegy by John Skelton written for Jane Scrope.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement I is false, but Statement II is true
items.explanation: Both statements are correct: Skelton wrote Colin Clout (c. 1522) attacking clerical corruption and Phyllyp Sparowe (c. 1505) mourning a pet sparrow.

items.title: Quiz Q#70 · Caedmon
items.stem: In which work by Caedmon does Caedmon appear as cowherd at Whitby who sings the hymn after a dream?
items.explanation: Caedmon (The cowherd at Whitby who sings the hymn after a dream) is a key figure in Caedmon's Caedmon’s Hymn.

items.title: Quiz Q#71 · Caedmon
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Now we must praise the Guardian of heaven"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Caedmon's Caedmon’s Hymn (late 7th century).

items.title: Quiz Q#72 · Caedmon
items.stem: Which nine-line Old English alliterative poem, preserved in Bede's Ecclesiastical History, is the earliest recorded English poem and praises God as the 'Guardian of the heavenly kingdom' (*heofonrices Weard*)?
items.explanation: Caedmon's Hymn (late 7th century) is the earliest surviving Old English poem, miraculously composed by an illiterate cowherd at Whitby Abbey.

items.title: Quiz Q#73 · Bede
items.stem: In which work by Bede does Bede appear as monk who writes the history and closes it with his own life note?
items.explanation: Bede (The monk who writes the history and closes it with his own life note) is a key figure in Bede's Historia Ecclesiastica Gentis Anglorum.

items.title: Quiz Q#74 · Bede
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"If history records good things of good men"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Bede's Historia Ecclesiastica Gentis Anglorum (731).

items.title: Quiz Q#75 · Bede
items.stem: Which foundational Latin historical work in five books, completed in 731 CE by the Venerable Bede at Jarrow, chronicles the Christianization of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and records the story of Caedmon?
items.explanation: Bede's Historia Ecclesiastica Gentis Anglorum ('Ecclesiastical History of the English People', 731 CE) earned him the title 'Father of English History'.

items.title: Quiz Q#76 · King Alfred the Great
items.meta: The Medieval Age · King Alfred the Great
items.stem: Which extensive intellectual and educational program of the late 9th century, spearheaded by King Alfred the Great, aimed to restore Latin and vernacular literacy in Wessex by translating essential texts into Old English?
options: Translation of Gregory the Great’s Pastoral Care
items.explanation: King Alfred the Great's educational revival in the late 9th century aimed to rebuild English learning and church life after Viking destruction, producing vernacular translations of key texts.

items.title: Quiz Q#77 · King Alfred the Great
items.meta: The Medieval Age · King Alfred the Great
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"most necessary for all men to know"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in King Alfred the Great's Alfredian learning revival (late 9th century).

items.title: Quiz Q#78 · King Alfred the Great
items.meta: The Medieval Age · King Alfred the Great
items.stem: Which late 9th-century intellectual project under King Alfred the Great saw the translation of key works such as Gregory's Pastoral Care, Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, and the initiation of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle?
options: Translation of Gregory the Great’s Pastoral Care
items.explanation: The Alfredian educational revival of the 890s produced foundational Old English translations of Gregory, Boethius, Orosius, and the compilation of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

items.title: Quiz Q#79 · King Alfred the Great
items.meta: The Medieval Age · King Alfred the Great
items.stem: In the preface to which Old English translation did King Alfred lament the decay of Latin learning in England and outline his plan to translate 'certain books which are most necessary for all men to know' into the vernacular?
options: Gregory the Great’s Pastoral Care (Cura Pastoralis)
items.explanation: King Alfred's translation of Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care (Cura Pastoralis, c. 890) features his celebrated prose preface advocating vernacular education.

items.title: Quiz Q#80 · King Alfred the Great
items.meta: The Medieval Age · King Alfred the Great
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"word for word, sense for sense"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in King Alfred the Great's translation tradition including Gregory the Great’s Pastoral Care (c. 890-897).

items.title: Quiz Q#81 · King Alfred the Great
items.meta: The Medieval Age · King Alfred the Great
items.stem: Sent to English bishoprics with an 'aestel' (precious pointer) worth fifty mancuses, which famous vernacular translation by King Alfred features an influential prose preface addressed to Bishop Wærferth of Worcester?
options: Gregory the Great’s Pastoral Care (Cura Pastoralis)
items.explanation: King Alfred sent copies of his Old English translation of Gregory's Pastoral Care accompanied by an 'aestel' to all the major bishoprics in his kingdom.

items.title: Quiz Q#82 · Cynewulf
items.stem: In which work by Cynewulf does Christ appear as Lord who ascends and promises to remain with his people?
items.explanation: Christ (The Lord who ascends and promises to remain with his people) is a key figure in Cynewulf's Christ II.

items.title: Quiz Q#83 · Cynewulf
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"I shall never leave you"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Cynewulf's Christ II (9th century).

items.title: Quiz Q#84 · Cynewulf
items.stem: Which Old English religious poem in the Exeter Book, concluding with Cynewulf's runic signature, dramatizes the Ascension of Christ and his triumph over death?
items.explanation: Cynewulf's Christ II (The Ascension, 9th century) is based on a homily by Pope Gregory the Great and contains Cynewulf's runic acrostic.

items.title: Quiz Q#85 · Cynewulf
items.stem: In which work by Cynewulf does Constantine appear as emperor whose vision of the cross wins his battle?
items.explanation: Constantine (The emperor whose vision of the cross wins his battle) is a key figure in Cynewulf's Elene.

items.title: Quiz Q#86 · Cynewulf
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"unlocked the art of poesy"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Cynewulf's Elene (9th century).

items.title: Quiz Q#87 · Cynewulf
items.stem: Which 1,321-line Old English poem in the Vercelli Book, ending with Cynewulf's longest runic signature, recounts the Roman Empress Saint Helena's quest to find the True Cross in Jerusalem?
items.explanation: Cynewulf's Elene (9th century) is a celebrated narrative of the Invention of the Cross, combining epic heroic diction with Christian legend.

items.title: Quiz Q#88 · Cynewulf
items.stem: In which work by Cynewulf does Juliana appear as A Christian virgin of Nicomedia who chooses martyrdom?
items.explanation: Juliana (A Christian virgin of Nicomedia who chooses martyrdom) is a key figure in Cynewulf's Juliana.

items.title: Quiz Q#89 · Cynewulf
items.stem: In which Old English hagiographical poem by Cynewulf does a Christian maiden of Nicomedia endure torture and defy the devil Affricanus to preserve her faith and virginity?
items.explanation: Cynewulf's Juliana (preserved in the Exeter Book) depicts female spiritual heroism and concludes with Cynewulf's runic signature requesting prayers.

items.title: Quiz Q#90 · Cynewulf
items.stem: In which work by Cynewulf does Cynewulf appear as speaker who lists the apostles and asks for prayers?
items.explanation: Cynewulf (The speaker who lists the apostles and asks for prayers) is a key figure in Cynewulf's The Fates of the Apostles.

items.title: Quiz Q#91 · Cynewulf
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"the body's borrowed fineries will crumble away"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Cynewulf's The Fates of the Apostles (9th century).

items.title: Quiz Q#92 · Cynewulf
items.stem: Which short Old English poem of 122 lines in the Vercelli Book recounts the missionary journeys, martyrdoms, and deaths of the twelve disciples, authenticated by Cynewulf's runic signature?
items.explanation: The Fates of the Apostles (9th century) is a martyrological catalogue poem serving as a prayer for Cynewulf's salvation.

items.title: Quiz Q#93 · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.stem: In which work by Ælfric of Eynsham does Aelfric appear as monk and mass priest who turns Latin teaching into English sermons?
items.explanation: Aelfric (The monk and mass priest who turns Latin teaching into English sermons) is a key figure in Ælfric of Eynsham's Catholic Homilies.

items.title: Quiz Q#94 · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The love that loves God is not idle"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ælfric of Eynsham's Catholic Homilies (c. 989-993).

items.title: Quiz Q#95 · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.stem: Which two-series collection of eighty Old English homilies, compiled around 990–995 CE, was designed to provide unlearned priests with orthodox vernacular sermons for Sundays and feast days?
items.explanation: Aelfric of Eynsham's Catholic Homilies (Sermones Catholici, c. 990–995) established standard Late West Saxon alliterative prose during the Benedictine Reform.

items.title: Quiz Q#96 · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.stem: In which work by Ælfric of Eynsham does Aelfric appear as teacher who explains Latin grammar in English?
items.explanation: Aelfric (The teacher who explains Latin grammar in English) is a key figure in Ælfric of Eynsham's Grammar.

items.title: Quiz Q#97 · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.stem: Which pioneer textbook, composed around 995 CE alongside a Latin-English Glossary and Colloquy, is the first Latin grammar written in a vernacular European language?
items.explanation: Aelfric's Grammar (Excerptiones de Arte Grammatica Anglice) was written to instruct young monastic novices in Latin fundamentals using Old English explanations.

items.title: Quiz Q#98 · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.stem: In which work by Ælfric of Eynsham does Aelfric appear as author, writing a third collection after the two homily series?
items.explanation: Aelfric (The author, writing a third collection after the two homily series) is a key figure in Ælfric of Eynsham's Lives of Saints.

items.title: Quiz Q#99 · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Ælfric of Eynsham
items.stem: Which collection of Old English narrative sermons, written between 996 and 997 CE in rhythmic, alliterative prose, celebrates the martyrdoms of saints venerated by monastic communities?
items.explanation: Aelfric's Lives of Saints (Passiones Sanctorum) contains vivid hagiographies of figures such as St. Edmund, St. Oswald, and St. George.

items.title: Quiz Q#100 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: In which work by Anonymous — Beowulf does Byrhtnoth appear as English leader who refuses tribute and dies in battle?
items.explanation: Byrhtnoth (The English leader who refuses tribute and dies in battle) is a key figure in Anonymous — Beowulf's The Battle of Maldon.

items.title: Quiz Q#101 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Heart shall be the keener"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Anonymous — Beowulf's The Battle of Maldon (after 991).

items.title: Quiz Q#102 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: Which late Old English heroic poem commemorates the defeat of the East Saxons against Viking invaders in 991 CE, containing Byrhtwold's famous speech on heroic defiance ('Mind must be the firmer, heart the bolder')?
items.explanation: The Battle of Maldon (c. 991–1000) depicts the death of Ealdorman Byrhtnoth due to his *ofermode* (over-courage/pride) in allowing the Vikings to cross the tidal causeway.

items.title: Quiz Q#103 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: In which work by Anonymous — Beowulf does The Dreamer appear as sinner who sees the vision and then prays?
items.explanation: The Dreamer (The sinner who sees the vision and then prays) is a key figure in Anonymous — Beowulf's The Dream of the Rood.

items.title: Quiz Q#104 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"I saw a wondrous tree"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Anonymous — Beowulf's The Dream of the Rood (8th-10th century).

items.title: Quiz Q#105 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: Which visionary Old English religious poem in the Vercelli Book presents the Cross itself speaking as a loyal warrior, recounting how it held the young hero Christ during the Crucifixion?
items.explanation: The Dream of the Rood (10th century, with fragments inscribed on the 8th-century Ruthwell Cross) is a masterpiece of Christian alliterative poetry merging Germanic heroic ethos with Christian devotion.

items.title: Quiz Q#106 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: In which work by Anonymous — Beowulf does The Seafarer appear as A sailor speaker who weighs sea hardship against earthly joy?
items.explanation: The Seafarer (A sailor speaker who weighs sea hardship against earthly joy) is a key figure in Anonymous — Beowulf's The Seafarer.

items.title: Quiz Q#107 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"I can sing a true song"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Anonymous — Beowulf's The Seafarer (before c. 970).

items.title: Quiz Q#108 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: Which 124-line Old English elegy in the Exeter Book contrasts the bitter physical hardships of winter voyages on icy northern seas with the hollow luxuries of city life on land?
items.explanation: The Seafarer (10th century) uses the perils of ocean voyage as an allegory for Christian peregrinatio (spiritual exile in the transitory earthly world).

items.title: Quiz Q#109 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: In which work by Anonymous — Beowulf does The Wanderer appear as An exile who speaks of loss, ruin, and wisdom?
items.explanation: The Wanderer (An exile who speaks of loss, ruin, and wisdom) is a key figure in Anonymous — Beowulf's The Wanderer.

items.title: Quiz Q#110 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Where is the horse gone"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Anonymous — Beowulf's The Wanderer (before c. 970).

items.title: Quiz Q#111 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: Which haunting Old English elegy in the Exeter Book depicts an *earth-stepper* (*eardstapa*) mourning his lost lord and mead-hall companions, meditating *ubi sunt* on the ruin of earthly glory?
items.explanation: The Wanderer (10th century) is a profound meditation on mutability, exile, and the transience of worldly joy (*wyrd bið ful aræd*).

items.title: Quiz Q#112 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: In which work by Anonymous — Beowulf does Beowulf appear as A Geatish hero who later becomes king?
items.explanation: Beowulf (A Geatish hero who later becomes king) is a key figure in Anonymous — Beowulf's Beowulf.

items.title: Quiz Q#113 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: Which 3,182-line Old English epic in the Nowell Codex (Cotton Vitellius A.xv) narrates the heroic deeds of a Geatish warrior fighting Grendel, Grendel's mother, and a dragon?
items.explanation: Beowulf (c. 8th–10th century) is the pinnacle of Old English heroic poetry, exploring kingship, loyalty, and pagan-Christian tensions in heroic Scandinavia.

items.title: Quiz Q#114 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: In which work by Anonymous — Beowulf does Havelok appear as exiled prince of Denmark, raised as a poor boy?
items.explanation: Havelok (The exiled prince of Denmark, raised as a poor boy) is a key figure in Anonymous — Beowulf's Havelok the Dane.

items.title: Quiz Q#115 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Herknet to me, gode men"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Anonymous — Beowulf's Havelok the Dane (c. 1280-1290).

items.title: Quiz Q#116 · Anonymous — Beowulf
items.stem: Which early Middle English metrical romance in rhyming four-stress couplets tells the tale of a disinherited Danish prince raised as a scullion who regains his kingdom and marries Princess Goldborough?
items.explanation: Havelok the Dane (c. 1280) is a lively Middle English romance of the 'Matter of England', celebrating popular justice and rightful kingship.

items.title: Quiz Q#117 · Wulfstan
items.stem: In which work by Wulfstan does Wulfstan appear as Archbishop of York, preaching under the name Lupus, the wolf?
options: Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (“Sermon of the Wolf to the English”)
items.explanation: Wulfstan (Archbishop of York, preaching under the name Lupus, the wolf) is a key figure in Wulfstan's Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (“Sermon of the Wolf to the English”).

items.title: Quiz Q#118 · Wulfstan
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"here are witches and Valkyries"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Wulfstan's Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (“Sermon of the Wolf to the English”) (c. 1014).

items.title: Quiz Q#119 · Wulfstan
items.stem: Which fiery Old English homily, delivered in 1014 by Archbishop Wulfstan under the pseudonym 'Lupus', denounces English moral decay and interprets Viking raids as God's retribution?
options: Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (“Sermon of the Wolf to the English”)
items.explanation: Wulfstan's Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (1014) is a masterpiece of impassioned alliterative prose warning that the end of the world is near.

items.title: Quiz Q#120 · Dante Alighieri
items.stem: In which work by Dante Alighieri does Dante the pilgrim appear as poet as a traveler through the three worlds of the afterlife?
items.explanation: Dante the pilgrim (The poet as a traveler through the three worlds of the afterlife) is a key figure in Dante Alighieri's The Divine Comedy.

items.title: Quiz Q#121 · Dante Alighieri
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Dante Alighieri's The Divine Comedy (c. 1308-1321).

items.title: Quiz Q#122 · Dante Alighieri
items.stem: Which monumental Italian epic in terza rima (*Inferno*, *Purgatorio*, *Paradiso*) traces Dante's journey guided by Virgil and Beatrice through the three realms of the afterlife?
items.explanation: Dante's Commedia (c. 1308–1320) synthesize medieval scholastic philosophy, theology, and politics, exerting immense influence on Chaucer and later English literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#123 · Geoffrey of Monmouth
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Geoffrey of Monmouth
items.stem: In which work by Geoffrey of Monmouth does Brutus appear as A descendant of Aeneas who begins the line of British kings?
items.explanation: Brutus (A descendant of Aeneas who begins the line of British kings) is a key figure in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae.

items.title: Quiz Q#124 · Geoffrey of Monmouth
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Geoffrey of Monmouth
items.stem: Which Latin pseudo-historical chronicle (c. 1136) popularized Arthurian romance throughout Europe, introducing King Arthur, Merlin, Guinevere, and the concept of King Lear?
items.explanation: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae ('History of the Kings of Britain') shaped British mythology and was the primary source for Arthurian legends.

items.title: Quiz Q#125 · Orm
items.stem: In which work by Orm does Orm appear as canon who preaches and invents the spelling?
items.explanation: Orm (The canon who preaches and invents the spelling) is a key figure in Orm's Ormulum.

items.title: Quiz Q#126 · Orm
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Thiss boc iss nemmnedd Orrmulum"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Orm's Ormulum (c. 1170-1180).

items.title: Quiz Q#127 · Orm
items.stem: Which Middle English biblical verse collection of roughly 19,000 unrhymed lines, composed in the East Midlands dialect c. 1170, is celebrated for its idiosyncratic phonetic spelling using doubled consonants?
items.explanation: The Ormulum (c. 1170) is invaluable to historical linguists because Orm systematically doubled consonants after short vowels to guide proper English pronunciation.

items.title: Quiz Q#128 · Layamon
items.stem: In which work by Layamon does Layamon appear as priest narrator who names himself at the start?
items.explanation: Layamon (The priest narrator who names himself at the start) is a key figure in Layamon's Brut.

items.title: Quiz Q#129 · Layamon
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"An preost wes on leoden"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Layamon's Brut (c. 1190-1215).

items.title: Quiz Q#130 · Layamon
items.stem: Which early Middle English chronicle poem of 16,095 lines (c. 1190–1215), written in alliterative long lines by a Worcestershire parish priest, is the first English-language work to feature King Arthur and the Round Table?
items.explanation: Layamon's Brut (c. 1200), adapted from Wace's Roman de Brut, revived Old English alliterative meter and introduced Arthur as an English national hero.

items.title: Quiz Q#131 · John Wycliffe
items.stem: In which work by John Wycliffe does John Wycliffe appear as reformer whose circle is linked with the project?
options: English Bible associated with the Wycliffite translations
items.explanation: John Wycliffe (The reformer whose circle is linked with the project) is a key figure in John Wycliffe's English Bible associated with the Wycliffite translations.

items.title: Quiz Q#132 · John Wycliffe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"God lovede so the world"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Wycliffe's English Bible associated with the Wycliffite translations (c. 1382-1395).

items.title: Quiz Q#133 · John Wycliffe
items.stem: Which late 14th-century vernacular translation of the Latin Vulgate Scriptures into Middle English was produced by the Oxford theologian John Wycliffe and his Lollard followers?
options: English Bible associated with the Wycliffite translations
items.explanation: The Wycliffite Bible (c. 1382–1388) was the first complete English Bible, condemned by Archbishop Arundel's Constitutions of Oxford in 1408.

items.title: Quiz Q#134 · John Gower
items.stem: In which work by John Gower does Amans appear as lover who confesses, and who is revealed as old John Gower?
items.explanation: Amans (The lover who confesses, and who is revealed as old John Gower) is a key figure in John Gower's Confessio Amantis.

items.title: Quiz Q#135 · John Gower
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Of hem that written us tofore"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Gower's Confessio Amantis (c. 1390).

items.title: Quiz Q#136 · John Gower
items.stem: Which Middle English poem in 33,000 octosyllabic couplets is framed as a confession by an aging lover (*Amans*) to Genius, the priest of Venus, illustrating the Seven Deadly Sins through classical tales?
items.explanation: John Gower's Confessio Amantis ('The Lover's Confession', c. 1390) is his major English work, praised alongside Chaucer by Renaissance humanists.

items.title: Quiz Q#137 · John Gower
items.stem: In which work by John Gower does The Narrator appear as moral teacher who holds up a mirror to mankind?
items.explanation: The Narrator (The moral teacher who holds up a mirror to mankind) is a key figure in John Gower's Mirour de l’Omme.

items.title: Quiz Q#138 · John Gower
items.stem: Which 30,000-line Anglo-Norman French poem by John Gower (*Speculum Meditantis*) examines the conflict between the Virtues and Vices and laments the moral corruption of all three medieval estates?
items.explanation: Mirour de l'Omme ('Mirror of Man', c. 1376–1379) reflects Gower's multilingual mastery, written in French octosyllabic twelve-line stanzas.

items.title: Quiz Q#139 · John Gower
items.stem: In which work by John Gower does The Dreamer appear as speaker who sees the revolt as a beast allegory?
items.explanation: The Dreamer (The speaker who sees the revolt as a beast allegory) is a key figure in John Gower's Vox Clamantis.

items.title: Quiz Q#140 · John Gower
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Vox clamantis in deserto"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Gower's Vox Clamantis (c. 1381).

items.title: Quiz Q#141 · John Gower
items.stem: Which Latin elegiac poem in seven books by John Gower was written in response to the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, depicting the rebellious peasants as transformed into howling, destructive beasts?
items.explanation: Vox Clamantis ('Voice of One Crying', c. 1381) contains Gower's horrified eyewitness perspective on the 1381 uprising and Wat Tyler's rebellion.

items.title: Quiz Q#142 · William Langland
items.stem: In which work by William Langland does Will appear as dreamer whose visions make up the poem?
items.explanation: Will (The dreamer whose visions make up the poem) is a key figure in William Langland's Piers Plowman.

items.title: Quiz Q#143 · William Langland
items.stem: Which major Middle English alliterative dream-vision poem in passus sections depicts Will's pilgrimage through the 'Field Full of Folk' seeking Truth, Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest?
items.explanation: William Langland's Piers Plowman (c. 1370–1386, surviving in A, B, and C texts) is a sweeping social and spiritual allegory critiquing church and court corruption.

items.title: Quiz Q#144 · Giovanni Boccaccio
items.stem: In which work by Giovanni Boccaccio does Pampinea appear as woman who first proposes the country retreat and the storytelling?
items.explanation: Pampinea (The woman who first proposes the country retreat and the storytelling) is a key figure in Giovanni Boccaccio's Decameron.

items.title: Quiz Q#145 · Giovanni Boccaccio
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Umana cosa è aver compassione degli afflitti"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Giovanni Boccaccio's Decameron (c. 1349-1353).

items.title: Quiz Q#146 · Giovanni Boccaccio
items.stem: Which Italian masterpiece of vernacular prose contains one hundred tales told over ten days by seven young women and three men fleeing the Black Death in Florence to a countryside villa?
items.explanation: Boccaccio's Decameron (1349–1353) established European novella traditions and provided direct narrative sources for several of Chaucer's Canterbury Tales.

items.title: Quiz Q#147 · Julian of Norwich
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Julian of Norwich
items.stem: In which work by Julian of Norwich does Julian appear as writer who receives and explains the showings?
items.explanation: Julian (The writer who receives and explains the showings) is a key figure in Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love.

items.title: Quiz Q#148 · Julian of Norwich
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Julian of Norwich
items.stem: Which spiritual work, based on sixteen visionary showings received during a near-fatal illness in 1373 and surviving in Short and Long texts, is the earliest surviving book in English written by a woman?
items.explanation: Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love (c. 1395) is famous for its theology of divine maternal love and the reassuring phrase 'All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well'.

items.title: Quiz Q#149 · Margery Kempe
items.stem: In which work by Margery Kempe does Margery Kempe appear as visionary, called this creature, who dictates the life?
items.explanation: Margery Kempe (The visionary, called this creature, who dictates the life) is a key figure in Margery Kempe's The Book of Margery Kempe.

items.title: Quiz Q#150 · Margery Kempe
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Daughter, why have you forsaken me"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Margery Kempe's The Book of Margery Kempe (1501).

items.title: Quiz Q#151 · Margery Kempe
items.stem: Which vivid prose work, dictated by an East Anglian mystic who experienced loud weeping fits (*roaring*) and traveled on pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome, and Santiago, is regarded as the first autobiography in English?
items.explanation: The Book of Margery Kempe (c. 1436–1438) offers invaluable insights into late medieval lay piety, female visionary authority, and domestic life.

items.title: Quiz Q#152 · Petrarch
items.stem: In which work by Petrarch does Petrarch the speaker appear as poet who records love, guilt, and spiritual change?
items.explanation: Petrarch the speaker (The poet who records love, guilt, and spiritual change) is a key figure in Petrarch's Canzoniere.

items.title: Quiz Q#153 · Petrarch
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Voi ch'ascoltate in rime sparse il suono"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Petrarch's Canzoniere (c. 1327-1374).

items.title: Quiz Q#154 · Petrarch
items.stem: Which collection of 366 lyric poems (mostly sonnets) by Francesco Petrarch (*Rerum Vulgarium Fragmenta*) established the Petrarchan sonnet tradition celebrating idealized, unrequited love for Laura?
items.explanation: Petrarch's Canzoniere (1327–1368) popularized the fourteen-line octave/sestet sonnet form and courtly oxymorons that dominated Elizabethan poetry.

items.title: Quiz Q#155 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem: In which work by Anonymous — Gawain Poet does The Narrator appear as teacher who links courtesy with spiritual cleanness?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
items.explanation: The Narrator (The teacher who links courtesy with spiritual cleanness) is a key figure in Anonymous — Gawain Poet's Cleanness.

items.title: Quiz Q#156 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Clannesse whoso kyndly cowthe comende"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Anonymous — Gawain Poet's Cleanness (late 14th century).

items.title: Quiz Q#157 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem: Which 1,812-line alliterative Middle English poem in MS Cotton Nero A.x illustrates the virtue of spiritual and physical purity through biblical narratives of the Fall of Angels, Noah's Flood, Sodom and Gomorrah, and Belshazzar's Feast?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
items.explanation: Cleanness (or Purity, c. 1375–1400) uses vivid scriptural retellings to celebrate fidelity and courtesy before God.

items.title: Quiz Q#158 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem: In which work by Anonymous — Gawain Poet does The Narrator appear as preacher who links patience to the Beatitudes?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
items.explanation: The Narrator (The preacher who links patience to the Beatitudes) is a key figure in Anonymous — Gawain Poet's Patience.

items.title: Quiz Q#159 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem: Which 531-line alliterative Middle English poem by the Gawain Poet retells the biblical story of Jonah and the whale as a moral homily on yielding patiently to divine will?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
items.explanation: Patience (c. 1375–1400) opens with the Beatitudes and employs comic realism to dramatize Jonah's reluctant obedience to God.

items.title: Quiz Q#160 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem: In which work by Anonymous — Gawain Poet does The Dreamer appear as grieving father who lost his young child?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
items.explanation: The Dreamer (The grieving father who lost his young child) is a key figure in Anonymous — Gawain Poet's Pearl.

items.title: Quiz Q#161 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Perle, plesaunte to prynces paye"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Anonymous — Gawain Poet's Pearl (late 14th century).

items.title: Quiz Q#162 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem: Which intricate 1,212-line Middle English dream-vision poem, written in 101 twelve-line complex rhyming stanzas linked by concatenatio, depicts a grieving father encountering his deceased infant daughter as a crowned Queen of Heaven?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
items.explanation: Pearl (late 14th century) is a pinnacle of alliterative and stanzaic artistry, exploring theological consolation and the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard.

items.title: Quiz Q#163 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem: In which work by Anonymous — Gawain Poet does Sir Gawain appear as Arthur's nephew, who bears the pentangle and then the green girdle?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
items.explanation: Sir Gawain (Arthur's nephew, who bears the pentangle and then the green girdle) is a key figure in Anonymous — Gawain Poet's Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.

items.title: Quiz Q#164 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Hony soyt qui mal pence"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Anonymous — Gawain Poet's Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (1839).

items.title: Quiz Q#165 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem: Which alliterative Arthurian masterpiece, written in 101 stanzas concluding in a 'bob and wheel', tests Gawain's chivalric honor through a Beheading Game and Temptation scenes at Hautdesert castle?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
items.explanation: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (late 14th century) explores the pentangle virtues, courtly courtesy, and moral human imperfection.

items.title: Quiz Q#166 · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.meta: The Medieval Age · Anonymous — Gawain Poet
items.stem: Which fifth alliterative Middle English poem, preserved in MS Harley 2250 and recounting the miraculous preservation and baptism of a righteous pagan judge's body in St. Paul's Cathedral, is traditionally attributed to the Gawain Poet?
items.explanation: Saint Erkenwald (c. 1386) is an alliterative Middle English poem recounting Bishop Erkenwald's baptism of an uncorrupted pagan judge; scholars frequently attribute it to the Gawain/Pearl Poet based on dialectal and stylistic similarities.

items.title: Quiz Q#167 · John Mandeville
items.stem: In which work by John Mandeville does Sir John Mandeville appear as narrator, presented as a knight of St Albans?
items.explanation: Sir John Mandeville (The narrator, presented as a knight of St Albans) is a key figure in John Mandeville's Mandeville's Travels.

items.title: Quiz Q#168 · John Mandeville
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"little beasts called loyres"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Mandeville's Mandeville's Travels (c. 1357).

items.title: Quiz Q#169 · John Mandeville
items.stem: Which wildly popular 14th-century fictional travel narrative, claiming to be written by an English knight of St. Albans, describes journeys to the Holy Land, the Great Khan's realm, and the kingdom of Prester John?
items.explanation: Mandeville's Travels (c. 1357) was a medieval bestseller, combining genuine geographical lore with fantastical tales of monsters and marvels.

items.title: Quiz Q#170 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem: In which work by Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve) does Thomas Hoccleve appear as poet who defends his recovered wits?
items.explanation: Thomas Hoccleve (The poet who defends his recovered wits) is a key figure in Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)'s Dialogue with a Friend.

items.title: Quiz Q#171 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"And endid my compleinte in this manere"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)'s Dialogue with a Friend (c. 1420-1421).

items.title: Quiz Q#172 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem: Which autobiographical poem in rhyme royal by Thomas Hoccleve, forming part of his *Series* (c. 1420), depicts the poet discussing his mental illness, literary career, and anxieties about public opinion with a visiting counselor?
items.explanation: Hoccleve's Dialogue with a Friend (c. 1420) is remarkable for its candid disclosure of psychological depression, social stigma, and poetic vulnerability.

items.title: Quiz Q#173 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem: In which work by Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve) does Thomas Hoccleve appear as clerk who confesses misrule and asks for his fee?
items.explanation: Thomas Hoccleve (The clerk who confesses misrule and asks for his fee) is a key figure in Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)'s La Male Regle.

items.title: Quiz Q#174 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"O precious tresour incomparabile"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)'s La Male Regle (c. 1405-1406).

items.title: Quiz Q#175 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem: In which 1405 mock-penitential complaint in rhyme royal does Thomas Hoccleve, a clerk of the Privy Seal, confess his youthful debaucheries, tavern bills, and vanity to the God of Health, begging Lord Furnival for his unpaid salary?
items.explanation: La Male Regle de T. Hoccleve (1405) offers a lively, self-deprecating picture of bachelor life and bureaucratic poverty in late medieval London.

items.title: Quiz Q#176 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem: In which work by Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve) does Thomas Hoccleve appear as speaker who describes his illness and his return to health?
items.explanation: Thomas Hoccleve (The speaker who describes his illness and his return to health) is a key figure in Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)'s The Complaint.

items.title: Quiz Q#177 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"After that hervest inned had his sheves"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)'s The Complaint (c. 1419-1421).

items.title: Quiz Q#178 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem: Which poignant first-person poem by Thomas Hoccleve describes his recovery from a five-year bout of mental breakdown ('wild infirmity') and his distress at seeing former acquaintances avoid his gaze in the mirror?
items.explanation: Hoccleve's Complaint (c. 1419–1420) opens the Hoccleve Series with unprecedented psychological introspection.

items.title: Quiz Q#179 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem: In which work by Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve) does Thomas Hoccleve appear as anxious clerk who writes the book for the prince?
items.explanation: Thomas Hoccleve (The anxious clerk who writes the book for the prince) is a key figure in Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)'s The Regiment of Princes.

items.title: Quiz Q#180 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"My maistir Chaucer, flour of eloquence"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)'s The Regiment of Princes (c. 1411).

items.title: Quiz Q#181 · Thomas Hoccleve (Occleve)
items.stem: Which advice-to-princes manual (*De Regimine Principum*) in 5,463 lines of rhyme royal was written in 1411 for Prince Henry (future Henry V), famous for its affectionate portrait and eulogy of Geoffrey Chaucer?
items.explanation: Hoccleve's The Regiment of Princes (1411) includes the famous marginal illumination of Chaucer, mourning Chaucer as his 'worthy master and father reverend'.

items.title: Quiz Q#182 · John Lydgate
items.stem: In which work by John Lydgate does John Lydgate appear as monk narrator who moralizes each fall?
options: The Complaint of the Black Knight
items.explanation: John Lydgate (The monk narrator who moralizes each fall) is a key figure in John Lydgate's The Fall of Princes.

items.title: Quiz Q#183 · John Lydgate
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"To yive exaumple how this world doth varie"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Lydgate's The Fall of Princes (1494).

items.title: Quiz Q#184 · John Lydgate
items.stem: Which massive 36,000-line narrative poem in rhyme royal by John Lydgate, written for Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester (1431–1438), translates Boccaccio's De Casibus to moralize the tragic downfalls of famous rulers?
options: The Complaint of the Black Knight
items.explanation: Lydgate's The Fall of Princes established the de casibus tragedy genre in England, leading directly to the Elizabethan Mirror for Magistrates.

items.title: Quiz Q#185 · John Lydgate
items.stem: In which work by John Lydgate does The poet dreamer appear as narrator who overhears the knight and records his complaint?
options: The Complaint of the Black Knight
items.explanation: The poet dreamer (The narrator who overhears the knight and records his complaint) is a key figure in John Lydgate's The Complaint of the Black Knight.

items.title: Quiz Q#186 · John Lydgate
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"In May, when Flora, the fressh lusty quene"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Lydgate's The Complaint of the Black Knight (c. 1402).

items.title: Quiz Q#187 · John Lydgate
items.stem: Which courtly dream-vision poem by John Lydgate, written in imitation of Chaucer's Book of the Duchess, depicts a solitary narrator walking in a May garden and overhearing a faithful lover's lament?
options: The Complaint of the Black Knight
items.explanation: The Complaint of the Black Knight (c. 1402) was long attributed to Chaucer in early printed editions, reflecting Lydgate's status as Chaucer's primary 15th-century disciple.

items.title: Quiz Q#188 · John Lydgate
items.stem: In which work by John Lydgate does John Lydgate appear as monk who joins the pilgrims and tells the tale?
options: The Complaint of the Black Knight
items.explanation: John Lydgate (The monk who joins the pilgrims and tells the tale) is a key figure in John Lydgate's The Story of Thebes.

items.title: Quiz Q#189 · John Lydgate
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Lo, her the fyn of contek and debat"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Lydgate's The Story of Thebes (c. 1420-1422).

items.title: Quiz Q#190 · John Lydgate
items.stem: Which 4,716-line poem by John Lydgate (c. 1420) is framed as an additional Canterbury tale told by the monk Lydgate himself, who meets the pilgrims at Canterbury and recounts the tragedy of Oedipus and the destruction of Thebes?
options: The Complaint of the Black Knight
items.explanation: The Story of Thebes (c. 1420) was designed by Lydgate as an overt sequel to Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, following The Knight's Tale.

items.title: Quiz Q#191 · John Lydgate
items.stem: In which work by John Lydgate does The dreamer appear as poet who enters the temple and records the lovers' pleas?
options: The Complaint of the Black Knight
items.explanation: The dreamer (The poet who enters the temple and records the lovers' pleas) is a key figure in John Lydgate's The Temple of Glass.

items.title: Quiz Q#192 · John Lydgate
items.stem: Which dream-vision allegory by John Lydgate depicts the narrator entering a glass temple of Venus where troubled lovers—including a lady forced into an unsuitable marriage—pray for the goddess's counsel?
options: The Complaint of the Black Knight
items.explanation: The Temple of Glass (c. 1403) blends Chaucerian dream-allegory with Boethian philosophy, exploring love, fortune, and marriage.

items.title: Quiz Q#193 · John Lydgate
items.stem: In which work by John Lydgate does Prince Henry appear as patron, later Henry V, who commissioned the poem in 1412?
options: The Complaint of the Black Knight
items.explanation: Prince Henry (The patron, later Henry V, who commissioned the poem in 1412) is a key figure in John Lydgate's Troy Book.

items.title: Quiz Q#194 · John Lydgate
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"O myghty Mars, that wyth thy sterne light"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Lydgate's Troy Book (1513).

items.title: Quiz Q#195 · John Lydgate
items.stem: Which monumental 30,000-line Middle English poem, commissioned by Prince Henry in 1412 and completed in 1420, provides a comprehensive chronicle of the Trojan War based on Guido delle Colonne?
options: The Complaint of the Black Knight
items.explanation: Lydgate's Troy Book (1412–1420) is an ambitious national epic celebrating Henry V's imperial vision through the classical matter of Troy.

items.title: Quiz Q#196 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: In which work by Geoffrey Chaucer does Dreamer appear as sleepless narrator who listens to the mourning knight?
items.explanation: Dreamer (The sleepless narrator who listens to the mourning knight) is a key figure in Geoffrey Chaucer's The Book of the Duchess.

items.title: Quiz Q#197 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"She was lady of the forest"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Geoffrey Chaucer's The Book of the Duchess (1532).

items.title: Quiz Q#198 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which dream-vision elegy in octosyllabic couplets was composed by Chaucer around 1368–1369 to commemorate the death of Blanche, Duchess of Lancaster, presenting a grieving Man in Black comforted by the Dreamer?
items.explanation: The Book of the Duchess is Chaucer's earliest major poem, heavily influenced by French love visions by Machaut and Froissart.

items.title: Quiz Q#199 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: In which work by Geoffrey Chaucer does The Knight appear as Noblest pilgrim; veteran of 15 battles; tells the romance of Palamon and Arcite.?
items.explanation: The Knight (Noblest pilgrim; veteran of 15 battles; tells the romance of Palamon and Arcite.) is a key figure in Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales.

items.title: Quiz Q#200 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales (c. 1387-1400).

items.title: Quiz Q#201 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which crowning masterpiece of Middle English literature, begun around 1387 and left incomplete at 24 tales, brings together thirty pilgrims of diverse social estates journeying to Canterbury?
items.explanation: The Canterbury Tales is Chaucer's panoramic portrait of 14th-century English society, using a pilgrimage frame to unite diverse genres from fabliau to saint's life.

items.title: Quiz Q#202 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: In which work by Geoffrey Chaucer does Geffrey appear as bookish narrator and dreamer?
items.explanation: Geffrey (The bookish narrator and dreamer) is a key figure in Geoffrey Chaucer's The House of Fame.

items.title: Quiz Q#203 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Now herke, how hyt gooth to Fame"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Geoffrey Chaucer's The House of Fame (1484).

items.title: Quiz Q#204 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which dream-vision poem in three books of octosyllabic couplets depicts Chaucer being carried into the heavens by a garrulous golden eagle to visit the whimsical palace of Lady Fame?
items.explanation: The House of Fame (c. 1379–1380) is an ironic parody of Dante's Commedia, examining the arbitrariness of literary reputation and rumor.

items.title: Quiz Q#205 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: In which work by Geoffrey Chaucer does Narrator / Chaucer appear as poet performing penance for his past writings on love?
items.explanation: Narrator / Chaucer (The poet performing penance for his past writings on love) is a key figure in Geoffrey Chaucer's The Legend of Good Women.

items.title: Quiz Q#206 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"A thousand tymes have I herd men telle"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Geoffrey Chaucer's The Legend of Good Women (1532).

items.title: Quiz Q#207 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which dream-vision poem by Chaucer, introducing heroic couplets to English, contains a Prologue where the God of Love orders the poet to write legends of faithful women (like Cleopatra, Dido, and Medea) as penance for defaming women in Troilus and Criseyde?
items.explanation: The Legend of Good Women (c. 1385–1386) is notable for its court of the daisy in the Prologue and its defense of feminine fidelity.

items.title: Quiz Q#208 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: In which work by Geoffrey Chaucer does Narrator appear as poet studying love through old books?
items.explanation: Narrator (The poet studying love through old books) is a key figure in Geoffrey Chaucer's The Parliament of Fowls.

items.title: Quiz Q#209 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The lyf so short, the craft so long"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Geoffrey Chaucer's The Parliament of Fowls (1478).

items.title: Quiz Q#210 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which 699-line dream-vision in rhyme royal, composed for Saint Valentine's Day (c. 1382), depicts birds of all ranks assembled before Nature to choose their mates, debated by three noble eagles?
items.explanation: The Parliament of Fowls is the first known literary text to link Valentine's Day with romantic courtly love.

items.title: Quiz Q#211 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: In which work by Geoffrey Chaucer does Troilus appear as A noble Trojan prince and faithful lover?
items.explanation: Troilus (A noble Trojan prince and faithful lover) is a key figure in Geoffrey Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde.

items.title: Quiz Q#212 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"O moral Gower, this book I directe"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Geoffrey Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (1483).

items.title: Quiz Q#213 · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Which tragic verse romance in five books of rhyme royal, dedicated to 'moral Gower' and 'philosophical Strode', adapts Boccaccio's Il Filostrato to narrate the ill-fated love of Troilus and Criseyde in besieged Troy?
items.explanation: Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1385) is regarded as Chaucer's narrative masterpiece, celebrated for deep psychological nuance and philosophical reflection on Boethian fate.

items.title: Quiz Q#214 · Thomas Malory
items.stem: In which Arthurian prose romance by Sir Thomas Malory does King Arthur establish the fellowship of the Round Table and meet his fate in the final battle on Salisbury Plain?
options: Sir Gawain and the Carl of Carlisle
items.explanation: King Arthur is the tragic monarch whose rise and fall fill Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte Darthur (completed c. 1470, printed 1485).

items.title: Quiz Q#215 · Thomas Malory
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"this noble and joyous book"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Thomas Malory's Le Morte Darthur (1485).

items.title: Quiz Q#216 · Thomas Malory
items.stem: Which monumental English prose romance, completed around 1469–1470 while the author was imprisoned and published by William Caxton in 1485, was rediscovered in 1934 in the Winchester College manuscript?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
items.explanation: Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte Darthur, printed by Caxton in 1485, was rediscovered in 1934 in the Winchester Manuscript (British Library Add. MS 59678).

items.title: Quiz Q#217 · William Caxton
items.stem: In his famous prologue to which translation does William Caxton reflect on the mutability and regional dialects of English, narrating the comical anecdote of a northern merchant asking for 'egges' in Kent?
options: Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye
The Dictes or Sayengis of the Philosophres
items.explanation: In his 1490 Prologue to Virgil's Eneydos, Caxton famously highlights the dialectal variety of English through the story of a merchant who asked for 'egges' and was refused by a housewife who only recognized 'eyren'.

items.title: Quiz Q#218 · William Caxton
items.stem: Which famous 1490 prologue by William Caxton humorously illustrates the dialectal instability of late 15th-century English through the story of a northern merchant refused food by a housewife because he asked for 'egges' instead of 'eyren'?
options: Introduction of the printing press to England in 1476
First printing of Le Morte Darthur in 1485
items.explanation: Caxton's Prologue to Eneydos (1490) is a celebrated milestone in English historical linguistics, showing Caxton's deliberate choice of standard London English for print.

items.title: Quiz Q#219 · William Caxton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Emprynted by me William Caxton"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Caxton's Introduced printing press to England in 1476 (1476).

items.title: Quiz Q#220 · William Caxton
items.stem: In which year did William Caxton establish England's first movable-type printing press at the Sign of the Red Pale in Westminster, producing early printed works such as The Dictes or Sayengis of the Philosophres?
options: First printing of Le Morte Darthur in 1485
Introduction of the printing press to England in 1476
items.explanation: William Caxton introduced the printing press to England in late 1476 at Westminster, transforming English literary culture and printing Chaucer, Gower, and Malory.

items.title: Quiz Q#221 · William Caxton
items.stem: Which monumental Arthurian prose work, written by Sir Thomas Malory, was organized into twenty-one books and printed by William Caxton at Westminster on 31 July 1485?
options: First printing of Le Morte Darthur in 1485
Introduction of the printing press to England in 1476
items.explanation: Caxton printed Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte Darthur on 31 July 1485, establishing the 21-book structure that became the standard reading edition for centuries.

items.title: Quiz Q#222 · William Caxton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"many noble and dyvers gentylmen"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Caxton's printed Le Morte Darthur in 1485 (1485).

items.title: Quiz Q#223 · William Caxton
items.stem: Whose manuscript compilation of Arthurian romances, completed around 1469–1470 and surviving in the Winchester Manuscript, was divided into twenty-one books by William Caxton when he first printed it in 1485?
options: Introduction of the printing press to England in 1476
First printing of Le Morte Darthur in 1485
items.explanation: Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte Darthur was printed by William Caxton on 31 July 1485; Caxton famously reorganized Malory's eight romances into twenty-one books.

items.title: Quiz Q#224 · John Skelton
items.stem: In which work by John Skelton does Colin Clout appear as plain wandering voice of common complaint?
items.explanation: Colin Clout (The plain wandering voice of common complaint) is a key figure in John Skelton's Colin Clout.

items.title: Quiz Q#225 · John Skelton
items.stem: In which fearless satirical poem in short, rhyming Skeltonics does John Skelton create a plain-spoken wandering rustic who reports the widespread public resentment against Cardinal Wolsey and clerical corruption?
items.explanation: John Skelton's Colin Clout (c. 1522) gave voice to popular grievances against church prelates, inspiring Edmund Spenser's persona in The Shepheardes Calender.

items.title: Quiz Q#226 · John Skelton
items.stem: In which work by John Skelton does Jane Scrope appear as young woman at Carrow whose sparrow has been killed?
items.explanation: Jane Scrope (The young woman at Carrow whose sparrow has been killed) is a key figure in John Skelton's Phyllyp Sparowe.

items.title: Quiz Q#227 · John Skelton
items.stem: Which playful mock-elegy by John Skelton, written in short, tumbling Skeltonic verses, depicts young Jane Scrope at Carrow Priory mourning her pet bird killed by Gib the cat, parodically combining the Roman Catholic Requiem Mass with love poetry?
items.explanation: Phyllyp Sparowe (c. 1505) is Skelton's most delightful lyric poem, praised by Coleridge as an exquisite piece of fancy.

items.title: Quiz Q#228 · John Skelton
items.stem: In which work by John Skelton does Parrot appear as caged bird whose broken, learned speech carries the satire?
items.explanation: Parrot (The caged bird whose broken, learned speech carries the satire) is a key figure in John Skelton's Speke, Parrot.

items.title: Quiz Q#229 · John Skelton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"But moveatur terra, let the world wag"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Skelton's Speke, Parrot (c. 1521).

items.title: Quiz Q#230 · John Skelton
items.stem: Which cryptic political satire by John Skelton (c. 1521) uses a pampered, multilingual caged bird speaking in riddles, proverbs, and macaronic phrases to deliver a scathing coded attack on Cardinal Wolsey?
items.explanation: Speke, Parrot is Skelton's most complex and obscure satire, using avian mimicry and prophetic lamentation to critique political tyranny.

items.title: Quiz Q#231 · John Skelton
items.stem: In which work by John Skelton does Drede appear as fearful dreamer who wants favor and meets the court vices?
items.explanation: Drede (The fearful dreamer who wants favor and meets the court vices) is a key figure in John Skelton's The Bowge of Court.

items.title: Quiz Q#232 · John Skelton
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"In autumpne, whan the sonne in Virgine"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Skelton's The Bowge of Court (c. 1499).

items.title: Quiz Q#233 · John Skelton
items.stem: Which allegorical court satire by John Skelton, written in rhyme royal, depicts a fearful dreamer named Drede boarding a ship called 'Court Rations' (*Bouge of Court*) where he encounters threatening vices like Favell, Harvy Hafter, and Dyssymulation?
items.explanation: The Bowge of Court (c. 1499) exposes the paranoia, flattery, and treachery of life at the Tudor court of Henry VII.
